Americans should expect more technology outages and disruptions as companies and government agencies replace aging systems, the top US intelligence official said on Sunday.
“And as part of that ongoing upgrade, we are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNN’s “State of the Union” program. “That is going to happen.”
Clayton was interviewed on Sunday morning news programs days after President Donald Trump attributed a recent spate of technology failures to upgrades of companies’ technology systems. Clayton said the upgrades were necessary to improve performance and cybersecurity as technological advances strain older systems.
A string of technology failures this month disrupted critical US systems, including a nationwide halt to air travel, a Microsoft outage that hit email services, a technical glitch that affected several major banks and a temporary disruption to the National Security Agency’s network.
Speaking on the ABC program “This Week,” Clayton reiterated his previous statements that those outages were not the result of coordinated or state-sponsored actions, attributing them to technical upgrades.
Clayton declined to discuss specifics of separate reports of cyberattacks on the FBI and Department of Agriculture, saying he expects investigators to provide answers “in due course.”

Next Plc said an online supplier suffered a breach that allowed unauthorized access to certain data relating to the retailer, the latest in a string of UK companies to be caught in cyberattacks.
The affected information is benign and can’t be used to facilitate fraud against customers or the company, the clothing and homeware retailer said Monday. No customer personal data has been compromised, it said.
Next is confident that its own systems haven’t been compromised but said it’s “treating the matter with the utmost seriousness.” The retailer did not identify the supplier or specify what data had been accessed. It said it’s working with the supplier, law enforcement and relevant regulatory authorities as it continues to look into the nature and scope of the incident.
Read more: ASOS Says Cyberattack May Have Compromised Customer Data
The disclosure adds to growing concerns over cyber risks facing the retail industry. Marks & Spencer Plc and the Co-op were targeted in a wave of attacks in 2025 that caused significant disruption, while Asos Plc said a breach of third-party communications platforms last month may have compromised customer data.
Cyberattacks have also spilled into retailers’ physical infrastructure. Hackers targeted internet-connected refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets in October, while a second wave affected supermarkets across several other European countries.

The man accused of sparking last year’s deadly Palisades Fire was found guilty of arson charges after his first federal case earlier this year ended in a mistrial.
Jurors on Friday convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, of lighting a fire on Jan. 1, 2025, that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up Jan. 7, becoming one of the most destructive wildfires in California history. The Palisades Fire killed 12 people as it incinerated entire neighborhoods in Los Angeles and Malibu.
Rinderknecht pleaded not guilty to federal charges of destruction of property by means of fire and arson. The scope of the first charge was narrowed to only include the Jan. 1 blaze, known as the Lachman Fire, and the second addresses the Palisades Fire. He was convicted on both charges.
Related: Wildfires Causing $1 Billion in Damage Have Jumped in Frequency in US
With little apparent reaction, Rinderknecht gave his attorneys hugs before leaving the courtroom. The verdict was delivered on the third day of deliberation.
Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in LA, said the verdict was a “testament of the hard work” his team put into the case. He said he was “intimately familiar” with the strength of the evidence and was happy with the jury that convicted Rinderknecht.
Rinderknecht’s attorney Steve Haney said in a statement they were disappointed in the verdict but respected the jury process.
“After a lengthy deliberation, they clearly gave this case a great deal of consideration,” Haney said. Regarding an appeal, he said they would review all the options at the right time.
Related: LA Wildfire Smoke Exposed 7 Million to Dangerous Toxic Metals
Rinderknecht is set to be sentenced March 17, 2027. Each count carries a mandatory minimum of five years and a maximum of 20 years in federal prison.
Prosecutors continued to pursue the case after Rinderknecht’s first jury deadlocked 10 to 2 in favor of acquittal after a two-week trial in June. They dropped a third charge of timber set afire when they filed a new indictment for the retrial. Essayli said he believed the first jury acted improperly and appeared to consider things in their decision that weren’t presented as evidence during the trial.
Juror Says Rinderknecht’s Own Testimony Pointed to A Guilty Verdict
Juror No. 3, who only wanted to be identified by his first name Cameron, said he was the only person who felt Rinderknecht was not guilty at the start of deliberations. Another person was undecided, and the rest of the 10 jurors believed Rinderknecht was guilty.
“It took a lot for me to be convinced otherwise,” he said. “After listening to every single point, I do now agree that he’s guilty.”
Cameron said he initially had concerns about a technical review conducted by a defense expert witness, who argued the government had gotten the origin area of the fire wrong. He said there was a “lack of information” presented to the jury about the technical review.
In the end, it was Rinderknecht’s own testimony that was the strongest piece of evidence pointing to a guilty verdict, he said.

The FBI is investigating a suspected breach of a nationwide database used by federal, state and local law enforcement agencies to share criminal justice information, CNN reported on Nov. 20, citing two people briefed on the investigation.
The apparent compromise of the National Crime Information Center database would mark the second intrusion involving an FBI system in recent months and the latest in a string of cyber incidents that have alarmed US officials over the past week.
The agency did not respond to a request for comment from Reuters.
The FBI database is used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to store and share information on warrants, criminal histories and background checks.
Previous high-profile cyber disruptions over the past week have included a global outage affecting hundreds of millions of Microsoft users and a nationwide halt to air travel that disrupted more than 18,000 flights.
A September breach by a digital extortion group known as “ShinyHunters” accessed an FBI jobs website, compromising data on current and former FBI employees.

Missouri’s budget crisis didn’t come out of nowhere
Years of tax cuts, rising spending and dwindling reserves have left Missouri facing billions in potential budget reductions.
Missouri Gov. Mike Parson during his State of the State address on Jan. 19, 2022 (Tim Bommel/Missouri House Communications).
Nearly a decade ago, then-Auditor Nicole Galloway issued a stark warning.
Her February 2018 budget stress test found Missouri increasingly dependent on individual income taxes and ill-equipped to weather an economic downturn.
“If there are economic bumps in the road ahead,” she said, “our state is not prepared.”
The report got a round of news stories. Then everyone moved on. Five months later, then-Gov. Mike Parson signed legislation touted as the largest single-year income tax cut in Missouri history.
Flash forward to last week, when a task force studying Missouri’s public school funding formula was told the legislature will likely need to cut $1.5 billion to $3.5 billion from what state agencies want to spend next year.
Missouri faces nearly $3 billion gap between spending requests and tax revenue
So what happened between the warnings and public discussion of a multibillion-dollar budget hole?
Federal pandemic assistance and unexpectedly strong tax collections helped Missouri build a massive surplus. By June 2023, the state’s general revenue fund held approximately $5.8 billion.
That gave lawmakers room to invest, increase spending and cut taxes.
So they did all three.
In 2022, Parson signed another income tax cut he called the largest in state history, estimated to reduce annual revenue by $764 million. A year later, lawmakers eliminated state income taxes on Social Security and public pension payments, at an estimated cost of $309 million a year.
Then, in 2025, Gov. Mike Kehoe signed legislation eliminating the state income tax on capital gains — profits from selling investments.
Originally estimated to cost $111 million annually, the exemption proved considerably more expensive. Its impact on fiscal 2026 revenue was later estimated at more than $500 million.
Meanwhile, spending grew.
Galloway’s successor, State Auditor Scott Fitzpatrick, documented just how quickly. From fiscal 2020 to 2025, general revenue grew 45.8%, while spending increased 53.4%. Inflation over that period was 24.5%.
Not all that spending growth was discretionary. Medicaid costs increased, pandemic assistance expired and maintaining existing programs became more expensive.
Nor is every appropriated dollar spent. Agencies leave money unused because of vacancies and project delays.
Still, Missouri was authorizing more spending than it collected annually and relying on the surplus to cover the difference. Now the money that made those budgets possible is nearly gone.
In December 2025, Fitzpatrick warned that continued deficit spending could exhaust the general revenue fund by fiscal year 2028. He repeated the warning in June, after lawmakers approved another budget exceeding projected revenue.

The Kehoe administration’s own budget instructions acknowledged that ongoing spending is projected to exceed recurring revenue by more than $1 billion.
As The Independent’s Rudi Keller reported last week, agencies are requesting approximately $16.5 billion in general revenue next fiscal year — nearly $3 billion more than the state expects to collect in the current fiscal year.

The Cardinals were a pleasant surprise in many ways in 2026, with emergent performances from Jordan Walker, JJ Wetherholt and Leo Bernal (among others) in the lineup and better-than-expected starting pitching from Michael McGreevy, Kyle Leahy and Andre Pallante. There is reason to be excited about both the lineup and the rotation moving forward.
But it is worth noting the aspect of the Cardinals’ roster that took a step back from 2025 to ‘26: the bullpen. Cardinals relievers put up a 4.40 ERA in 2026 (20th in MLB), which was roughly three-quarters of a run worse than the 3.74 they put up in 2025 (10th), and for that matter the 3.64 they notched in 2024 (seventh). In the past decade, only the 4.47 ERA of 2023 (23rd) was worse for the franchise.
Now, the Cardinals are in many ways focusing on compiling as much pitching as possible moving forward, to the point that it’s a signature plank of everything president of baseball operations Chaim Bloom and his staff are doing. But in the short term, St. Louis does need to see improvement from its bullpen. It’s tough for a young team to build up its confidence if its bullpen keeps giving up leads in the late innings. (The 2026 Cardinals tied for MLB’s third-most blown saves, with 30, and sixth-most relief losses, with 34).
So what does the Cardinals’ bullpen look like for 2027? Here are four key questions facing Bloom and company this offseason:
Whither Riley O’Brien?
In some ways, 2026 was a great season for O’Brien. He tied the great Mason Miller for the National League lead in saves with 38. He made the NL All-Star team. He even had a pretty cool entrance video at Busch Stadium. It’s all very impressive for a guy who, before 2025, was 30 years old and had thrown exactly 10 1/3 big league innings.
But it’s undeniable that O’Brien fell off as the season went along. He was a miserable 0-6 with a 5.11 ERA in the second half, and his walk rate nearly doubled after the break. He looked like a superstar in April; he looked pedestrian after that. O’Brien is still under team control for four more seasons – he’s 31 and still hasn’t hit arbitration yet – so the Cardinals are in no hurry to give up on him. But it seems unlikely he’ll just be handed the closer role on Opening Day, either.
Is Luis Gastelum ready to make the leap?
The Cardinals might be more excited about Gastelum than any other young pitcher on the roster, and if there’s a likely candidate to battle O’Brien for the closer spot, it would have to be him. Gastelum’s changeup is widely considered a best-in-class pitch; Major League batters hit .169 against it and whiffed on nearly half of their swings.
Gastelum had a truncated start to the season due to participating in the World Baseball Classic, and when he was first called up to St. Louis in July, there were some struggles, which some in the organization attributed to pitch tipping. After that, though, he was excellent, with a 2.31 ERA over his final 22 appearances. The walks are a little high, but his 10.8 K/9 rate will absolutely play, and there’s reason to think that will improve as he gets more reps. Gastelum has shut-down stuff, and if you’re looking for one Cardinals reliever to break out in 2027, he is an excellent candidate.

The book traces a journey through all seven continents, beginning with a solo trip to the American Southwest in March 2020 after a photography conference was cancelled and much of the world stopped moving.
Stern structures the book continent by continent. Each photograph appears alongside the full sensory record of the moment it was made. Readers encounter the smoky, fermented taste of kymyz offered inside a Kyrgyz yurt, frost crystals falling as a tent unzips on the Sary-Jaz Mountains at sunrise, and robusta coffee two hours after dawn in the rice paddies of Northwest Vietnam. At White Pocket in Arizona, standing on rock that pulsed terracotta and ochre beneath a cobalt sky, Stern made himself a promise about the role creative expression would play in the rest of his life.
The book's central tension is one of self-definition. Stern resists the label of landscape photographer, describing it as a box that felt polished, precise, and oddly impersonal. He calls himself a scenery enthusiast instead, arguing that scenery is not a view but a sensory event. That renaming required him to set aside the technical measures by which photographers are usually judged and to trust a creative voice he spent much of his life believing he did not have.
Jeff Stern stated, "I kept asking myself the same questions after every scene, and none of them were about aperture or shutter speed. They were: What did I hear? What did the ground feel like underfoot? I wrote this book because those questions changed what I was able to see, and I think they can do the same for anyone who spends time in nature – with or without a camera."
The book closes with the Five-Sense Lens, a framework Stern built from those recurring questions. Readers can try an interactive version of the Five-Sense Lens at https://sceneryenthusiast.com.

This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Seth Klarman’s Baupost Group disclosed in its latest 13F, filed November 13, that Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN | AMZN Price Prediction) was its largest holding at quarter-end. It made up 18.49% of a $5.05 billion reported portfolio. The filing lists 3.74 million shares worth about $933 million as of September 30. Baupost held its Amazon share count flat during the quarter.
How Amazon’s Portfolio Weight Rose Without a Purchase
Amazon’s weight rose from 16.48% in the June filing to 18.49% at the end of September, with the share count flat. A holding’s weight rises when it outperforms the rest of the book or when other positions shrink.
The filing clearly shows the second effect. Baupost cut its share counts in Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Union Pacific (NYSE:UNP) by more than 30% each. It also opened a new stake in Honeywell Aerospace (NASDAQ:HONA): 1.13 million shares worth about $175 million.
The filing shows a value investor who trimmed elsewhere and left his top position alone. Alphabet still sits at 6.41% of the portfolio and Union Pacific at 4.29%.
What Klarman Appears to See in AWS
Klarman built his reputation on buying with a margin of safety, so a stock trading near 25 times forward earnings as his top holding stands out. Amazon Web Services revenue grew 39%[1] year over year in the third quarter to $45.98 billion, its fastest pace in about five years.
AWS operating income reached $17.77 billion[1] versus $11.43 billion a year earlier, and consolidated operating income rose 61%. CEO Andy Jassy said “AWS investment is working”[1] and pointed to projected AWS growth “of over 40% both in 2027 and in 2028.”
That growth comes with a steep bill. Amazon plans roughly $220 billion[1] in capital spending for fiscal 2026, and trailing free cash burn sits near $42.4 billion.
Third-quarter GAAP EPS of $1.89[1] also came in below the $1.96 consensus. Sitting tight through all that suggests Baupost is valuing AWS earnings power several years out and accepting thin cash flow in the meantime.
What Retirement Investors Can Learn From Klarman’s Amazon Stake
Keep in mind that 13F data is outdated by design, as positions are reported roughly 45 days after quarter-end, and Amazon has moved since. Shares closed at $246.82 on November 20, down 7.44% over the past week but still up 6.93% year to date.
Position sizing is the bigger lesson here. Most investors trim a winner the moment it gets big, but Klarman let Amazon run to nearly a fifth of his reported portfolio while cutting other large positions.
For a retirement account, though, an 18% single-stock weight is aggressive, and a 13F only captures part of what Baupost manages. Investors studying the thesis can weigh it against their own risk tolerance and concentration limits.
Our Verdict on Klarman’s Amazon Conviction
Klarman’s Amazon position is worth following as a research signal, because it rests on measurable AWS acceleration and a willingness to wait. The test for anyone studying it is whether the $220 billion[1] expansion turns into the 40%-plus AWS growth Jassy projected.
If that happens, Baupost’s patience will look smart. If capex keeps exceeding cash flow, the margin of safety gets thinner.

The U.S. Army has planned to detonate about 9,700 pounds of deteriorating lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, roughly 57 miles north of Missouri. For what seemed like an incredibly long time, the women’s race at any ultra got far less attention than the men’s race. The Western States 100 — with its historic, record-setting performances by Ann Trason, Ellie Greenwood, Courtney Dauwalter, and this year, Jenn Lichter — was perhaps ahead of the rest when it came to recognizing the incredible performances by women.
It’s fitting, then, that “Raise the Bar,” a film by Hilary Yang and Carrie Highman, uses the 2025 Western States 100 as its backdrop to tell the story of four women runners — three elite and one non-elite — as they train and compete in the event. And there’s one thing that’s incredibly clear throughout the film: Women’s racing is where it is today because of the audacious, strong women who came before.
The four athletes in the film are nothing if not diverse in their backgrounds, running styles, and personalities. China’s Fu-Zhao Xiang returns after coming in second in 2024 and running the third-fastest time in the race’s history. Heather Jackson, a successful triathlete for 15 years who turned to trail running and gravel cycling, is chasing another top-10 spot after her seventh-place finish in 2024. Eszter Csillag, a Hungarian living in Hong Kong, is a mom of two young kids. She’s been third place at the race twice. Cindy Shepard of Portland, Oregon, a non-elite runner coached and mentored by ultrarunning legend Yassine Diboun, adds a refreshing dose of reality to a film genre almost exclusively obsessed with elites and the front of the pack. Her story reminds us that we do this largely for the love of the community and adventure, and not the pursuit of podiums.
History of Women in the Western States 100
At nearly 90 minutes, “Raise the Bar” has room to breathe. Not only does the film cover the current state of women at this iconic race, but it also does an excellent job of telling the robust and rich history of the Western States 100, a foot race founded in 1977 by “The Gang of Four,” including two women: Mo Livermore and Shannon Weil. The historic footage of the early years of the race offers a perspective on the oldest ultra in the U.S.
That history sets the stage for the women who spent the next several decades pushing the sport forward, a lineage brought to life in the film by voices like Dauwalter, Magda Boulet, Meghan Canfield, and Greenwood. But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?

Evaluate Your Effort, Distance, and Race Goals to Set Your Recovery Time
In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, says Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.
You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.
“There’s new research that shows the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris says. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still important to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.
With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:
If you raced well and feel well…
The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.
However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.
If you raced well but feel bad…
After a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris says. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.

When a certificate of deposit comes due, the bank gives you a short window to decide what happens next: let it renew at whatever the bank pays that day, or take the cash and move some of it into dividend stocks. On the rate side, the FDIC national average yield on a 12-month CD was 1.81%[1] as of November 1, 2026, up from 1.76% on October 1 and 1.64% on November 1, 2025. That number averages across banks. Some of the best online banks pay materially higher[1] rates.
What Happens in the Days After Your CD Matures
A CD is a time deposit. You hand a bank a fixed sum for a set term; the bank pays a stated annual percentage yield, and that rate remains locked until the term ends. At maturity, you get your principal back plus the interest earned. Only the term you buy has a fixed rate. The national average itself moves every month, so the next CD you open will carry whatever rate the bank sets at that point.
Maturity opens a grace period, typically 7 to 10 days, when you can take out the money, add to it, or change terms without penalty. If you do nothing, the bank usually rolls the balance into a new CD of the same length at its current rate, which may carry less favorable terms. Read the maturity notice before the window closes.
That rollover is where reinvestment risk shows up. The rate you locked in years ago is gone, and the new one may be higher or lower. The national average has moved both ways recently: it fell to a low of 1.52%[1] in March 2026 before climbing back to the current reading. Every renewal means taking whatever rate is on offer that day.
Two other limits matter. FDIC insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per FDIC-insured bank, for each account ownership category[2]. Anything above that line at a single bank, in the same ownership category, is uninsured if the bank goes. FDIC coverage also doesn’t protect your purchasing power from inflation. Cashing out a bank CD before maturity also costs an early withdrawal penalty set in the account agreement. Brokered CDs carry a different risk: if you sell one before maturity, you get the market price, which can be below what you paid.
Dividend Safety Has to Come Before Dividend Yield

This article looks at how much of Amazon’s profit came from gains on stocks and stakes it holds, and what a slide like Anthropic’s could mean for that profit.
The answer is a large share. Over the four quarters to September 2026, 40.1% of Amazon’s pre-tax income was non-operating income. That is profit from outside the business itself, such as gains on stocks and stakes a company owns. Almost all of it was gains on securities, $69.7 billion.
That is new for Amazon. From 2019 to 2022, non-operating items were a small net loss, -6.0% of pre-tax income. From 2023 to September 2025, they were 9.3% of pre-tax income. So Amazon’s reported profit now rises and falls with the prices of what it holds. The income statements do not show which holdings produced the gains. So we do not size any single one, Anthropic included.
Which Quarter Brought In Most Of The Gains?
Most of it came in one quarter. In the three months to June 2026, Amazon’s non-operating income was $53.4 billion. That was 66.0% of its pre-tax income. It was also the largest of any quarter since the start of 2019.
Net income that quarter was $62.6 billion. Operating income, the profit from selling goods and services, was $27.5 billion. So net income was 2.3 times operating income.
Amazon’s net income in the three months to June was 2.3 times its operating income. If Amazon is a big part of your savings, the profit it reports can drop fast when the stocks it holds fall. The state’s constitution was designed to insulate education leadership from partisan pressure. Critics question whether those safeguards are working as intended.
Missouri Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O'Laughlin — pictured during the inauguration of Gov. Mike Kehoe Jan. 13, 2025 — will step into a new role as interim commissioner of education Dec. 1 (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).
Missouri’s 1945 constitution put the selection of the state’s education commissioner in the hands of an appointed board, a change intended to insulate education leadership from partisan politics.
The State Board of Education’s decision last week to name Senate President Pro Tem Cindy O’Laughlin as interim commissioner has renewed questions about whether those safeguards are working as intended.
O’Laughlin, a Shelbina Republican, breaks from a tradition of career educators leading the department. Critics worry her appointment could bring partisan politics into an agency designed to operate independently.
“The Missouri Constitution includes an independent State Board of Education to keep politics out of the commissioner hiring process,” the Missouri State Teachers Association wrote in a statement Friday. “Today’s decision puts it right back in.”

The group endorsed a new constitution, approved by voters in 1945, which created an eight-person State Board of Education and the education commissioner position. Previously, the department’s chief was an elected superintendent of schools chosen on a partisan ballot.
A pamphlet circulated to voters at the time advertised that the constitution “takes the State Department of Education out of politics.”
“Education is so important that we don’t want it handled in a partisan fashion,” Duane Martin, an attorney whose law firm EdCounsel represents public school districts, told The Independent. “We want education policy for this state to be above partisan politics, and that insulation has been removed.”
State Board of Education President Brooks Miller has defended O’Laughlin’s appointment, pointing to her experience on a local school board, as a business owner and as a legislative leader. He said those skills will benefit the department and Missouri students.
Constitutional convention

France's economy is flashing fresh recession warnings as businesses delay decisions ahead of the 2027 election — but resilient industries, progress on the budget and lower energy costs could help keep growth positive.
Business activity declined to a six-month low in November, with manufacturing performing worse than the services sector, according to the S&P Global Purchasing Managers' Index published on Monday.
The French private sector is at its most pessimistic about the coming year since late 2012, excluding the months at the start of the pandemic, according to the survey, with job losses recorded for a seventh straight month.
Among the biggest challenges cited by companies were economic conditions, uncertainty, competition and cost pressures, while frail domestic demand is weighing on sales.
France is heading toward a closely watched presidential election in April 2027, with polling suggesting voters may favor candidates offering a break from the policies associated with incumbent President Emmanuel Macron.
Politico polling this year has consistently indicated the front-runner is far-right candidate Marine Le Pen, who has recently made efforts to appease financial market jitters over France's fiscal sustainability, but has failed to convince many analysts that she can stabilize the country's debt trajectory.
The latest PMI figures add to a run of economic woes for France this year, including a dramatic rise in government borrowing costs, a surprise outlook downgrade by ratings agency Fitch, and a tumbling stock market which has underperformed its European peers.
This has compounded a sense of crisis after hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets in October and November to protest underfunding in education, the cost of living and the state of public services and housing.
The latest PMI survey has meanwhile raised the odds of France entering a technical recession — two consecutive prints of negative GDP growth — in the fourth quarter, according to Joe Hayes, senior principal economist at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The next print will follow a 0.1% contraction in the third quarter, though a revised Q3 reading is due on Friday.
"The eurozone's second-largest economy is struggling with weak domestic demand, in part due to hesitancy from clients to commit to projects ahead of a highly uncertain election period next year," Hayes said.
"We've subsequently seen a rapid deterioration in business confidence these past few months as other long-standing issues, such as concerns about France's fiscal position, resurface as the election draws closer."
"It's also notable that output price inflation has slowed sharply in November. This suggests that company pricing power has diminished and further highlights the fragility of the French economy," Hayes added.

Who Pays P&G? The American Shopper In Four Lines
Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?
Nvidia is paid by cloud companies such as Google. The clouds are paid by companies such as Nike and P&G. Those companies are paid by you at the checkout. So the last question in the chain is the simplest one. Can the shopper keep paying?
We looked at Nike’s side of the chain in Nike Sells Shoes. Can It Stop Paying For AI? Here we look at the shopper.
Shoppers’ spending is growing faster than their income, and the difference is coming out of savings.
The shopper in four lines. Spending grew 2.5%, income 1.0%.
Source: Trefis, using FRED data. Income after taxes and inflation, and spending after inflation, compare September 2026 with September 2025. The savings rate is for September. Debt payments as a share of income are for the second quarter of 2026.
Americans now put aside 3.8% of what they earn after taxes, down from 5.1% a year earlier. If your own savings will one day have to cover your bills, what they pay you each year matters. The Trefis Income Solution owns 50 companies that have each paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row, and together they yield about 3 times what the S&P 500 pays. See the Income Solution.
Is The Shopper Overextended?
On savings, yes. On debt, no.
We compared today’s shopper with two moments worth remembering. One is mid-2007, just before the housing bust. The other is the end of 2019, before the pandemic. The savings rate, 3.8%, is close to mid-2007’s 2.7%. The debt picture looks more like 2019.
Source: Trefis, using FRED data. Savings rate: September 2026. Debt payments and late card payments: second quarter of 2026. Household debt: first quarter of 2026.
So this is not 2007. Households owe far less compared with their income. Late payments on credit cards are near normal. What is thin is the cushion of savings.
Revolving credit, mostly credit-card balances, did reach a record $1.37 trillion. It is up 4.2% in a year. That is slower than spending, which rose 6.3% before inflation. And people feel the strain. Consumer sentiment, a survey of how people feel about their money and the economy, was 48 in October. That is near its record low of 44.8, set in May.
How Long Can It Last?
About a year, before savings fall below 2007’s level.
Spending is growing 1.5 percentage points faster than income. Another year like this would take the savings rate from 3.8% to about 2.3%. That is below mid-2007’s 2.7%. After that, shoppers would either borrow more or spend less. Their light debts would allow them to borrow more.
If they spend less, P&G, Pepsi and Nike would feel it first. Then, one link at a time, it would reach their cloud bills, Google’s capital spending and Nvidia’s sales.
Two things will decide it. One is whether income grows faster if inflation cools. The other is whether the Fed cuts the cost of the borrowing that shoppers can still afford.
The line to remember: the American shopper is paying P&G out of savings, not debt. That is safer than in 2007. But at this pace, savings fall below 2007’s level in about a year.
Shoppers are learning what a thin cushion feels like. Your own money does not have to choose between growing and paying you as it goes.

Many shoppers look forward to Black Friday and Cyber Monday in anticipation of scoring a good deal or two. Adobe forecasts that consumers will spend over $15 billion online on Cyber Monday and $12.9 billion on Black Friday, making them two of the biggest shopping days of the year.
However, for some shoppers, these holidays can cost them more than they bargained for. A separate study from McAfee found a 91% year-over-year spike in the number of Americans reporting holiday shopping scams, and 60% of those who lost money lost at least $100.
"Black Friday and Cyber Monday create a perfect environment for scammers because consumers are actively looking for deals and often make quick purchasing decisions," said Michael Bruemmer, vice president of global data breach resolution and consumer protection at Experian.

3 common holiday shopping scams and how to avoid them
Holiday shopping scams can take on many forms and be easy to miss. Shoppers rushing to get their holiday shopping done at the lowest possible prices may be less likely to notice a scam or vet purchases as carefully as they normally would.
Some of the most common holiday shopping scams include:
Phishing emails and text messages
Shoppers may receive fake text messages or emails from scammers posing as retailers or shipping companies.
"Phishing emails and text messages will always be a popular tactic for fraudsters, and the messages may appear to come from well-known retailers, shipping companies, or payment providers and are often designed to steal login credentials or financial information," said Bruemmer.
Legitimate retailers and shipping companies will never ask shoppers to share personal information via email or text. If you receive a text message or email that you suspect could be a phishing scheme, you can report this scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
Gift card scams
Gift card scams occur year-round, but they tend to ramp up during the holiday season. Scammers may try to sell gift cards online at a "discount" and never send them, or sell cards whose balances have already been drained. Some scammers may even photograph gift cards in stores and wait for someone to purchase and load the card, then drain the balance.
When making any gift card purchases this holiday season, only purchase cards from trusted retailers or directly on the retailer's website rather than via a third-party website.
Fake online stores
Scammers may build fake websites that imitate trusted retailers to trick consumers into sharing their personal information. These websites can look quite convincing, but there are a few red flags to watch for that can help shoppers determine whether a website is legitimate.
This includes mobile apps or websites that ask shoppers to grant access to your contacts, text messages, stored passwords, or payment information. Other signs, such as misspelled words on the website or in the URL, discounts that are too good to be true, and limited or missing contact information, can also indicate that a website is fraudulent.
Shoppers can rely on tools such as Scamwise, ScamAdviser, and Google Safe Browsing to check whether a website is suspicious and receive alerts before visiting a fraudulent site.

What Would A Short Seller Say About IBM Stock?
Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?
International Business Machines (IBM) stock returned -17.6%, dividends included, in the year to Monday, November 23. The S&P 500 returned 12%. Yet the business grew. Revenue rose 6.8% in the four quarters to September 2026. The operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 18.3% from 17.7% a year earlier.
Management did not blame an outside cause. On its October 21 call, it spoke of “strength across our portfolio and solid execution”. A short seller, someone who bets a stock will keep falling, would still push on three points. Rivals grow faster, IBM’s growth has been uneven, and its debt is heavier than the market’s.
Are IBM’s rivals growing faster?
Yes, three of the four peers we compare grew faster. Alphabet grew revenue 22.2% and Microsoft grew 17.9%. Amazon.com grew 15.4%. Only Accenture grew about as slowly as IBM, at 6.5%. Each company is measured over its own latest four quarters.
IBM stock lost 17.6% in a year, dividends included, even as its revenue grew 6.8%. If IBM is a large part of your savings and you live on its dividend, that is a long fall to sit through. The Trefis Income Solution pays a dividend yield about 3 times the S&P 500’s, from 50 companies that have paid dividends for at least 10 years in a row. See what it pays.
Slow sales growth is not a long-running problem at IBM. Yearly growth rose from 1.1% in the four quarters to September 2023 to 6.8% now. The quarters were uneven, though. Revenue grew 12.2% in the quarter to December 2025 and 9.5% in the quarter to March 2026. It then grew 1.1% in the quarter to June and 4.7% in the quarter to September.
What did IBM’s managers say about the uneven quarters?
Management named its own cause for the soft June quarter. “Last quarter, it impacted our software growth by 4-5 points when we were down double-digit transactional,” a manager said.
Transaction processing (TP) software then grew 10% in the September quarter. “I do not expect double-digit performance in TP to keep going,” a manager said candidly. Management also said about a quarter of the software speed-up came from deals that slipped from earlier quarters. So part of the September bounce was timing.
Does the cash show strain for an owner?
The payout does not. Free cash flow, the cash left after running the business and buying equipment, was $14 billion over four quarters. Dividends took $6.3 billion and buybacks about $1 billion.
Debt is the softer spot. It stood at $67.1 billion, up from $59 billion five years earlier. That equals 30.5% of IBM’s market value, against 20.2% for the S&P 500.
What is the case for holding IBM?
The stock is cheaper while profit rose. At Monday’s close, IBM traded at 19.7 times its past year’s earnings, below 21.2 times for the S&P 500. At the end of September 2025, it traded at 33.3 times. Operating income rose from $11.5 billion to $12.8 billion over that year. Net income rose faster, helped by a December 2025 quarter in which it was larger than operating income.

Your Exxon Dividend Needs Only About $59 Oil
Today’s big story: Nvidia Added $954 Billion In A Day. Is Jensen Huang Too Big To Fire?
Oil has fallen, and oil stocks have fallen with it. WTI crude, the main U.S. oil price, fell 17.3% from $108.21 on Oct 16 to $89.53 on Nov 17. Exxon Mobil stock fell 14.4% in the month to Monday’s close. Chevron fell 11.6%.
So what oil price do their payouts actually need? On each company’s own record since 2015, Exxon’s dividend and share buybacks together need WTI to average about $79 a barrel over a year. Chevron’s need about $80. The dividend alone needs much less. That line is about $59 for Exxon and about $65 for Chevron.
Oil’s latest print is 12.9% above Exxon’s full-payout line. It is 11.3% above Chevron’s. On this measure, both payouts are still covered. Our read is that the dividends are the safe part, and the buybacks are what cheaper oil would test.
How much of their cash do the payouts use today?
Free cash flow is the cash a company keeps after paying for its wells, plants and other capital spending. In the four quarters to September, oil averaged $78.87 a barrel. That is close to the full-payout lines above, about $79 for Exxon and $80 for Chevron.
In those months, Exxon’s free cash flow covered its dividend 2.5 times. Its dividends plus buybacks used 87.9% of free cash flow. Chevron’s payouts used 73.3%.
Exxon Mobil’s cash covered its quarterly checks to holders 2.5 times over the past year, even as the stock fell 14.4% in a month. If those checks pay your bills, the falling share price is the part you have to sit through. The wider market did not drive Monday’s selling. The SPDR S&P 500 fund rose 4.7% that day, while Exxon fell 1.9%.
How did we find the oil price each payout needs?
We set each company’s free cash flow for every calendar year from 2015 to 2025 against that year’s average WTI price. A straight line fits Exxon’s record closely. Each $1 a barrel was worth about $1 billion of Exxon’s yearly free cash flow. For Chevron, each $1 was worth about $714 million.
We then found the yearly oil price at which that cash equals the latest twelve months of payouts. A check on 47 single quarters gives nearly the same lines. It puts Exxon’s full-payout line at $78.34 and Chevron’s at $78.08.
Today’s companies did better than the old record predicts. At the past four quarters’ $78.87 oil, the fit expected $37.3 billion of free cash flow from Exxon. Exxon produced $43 billion. The fit expected $23.9 billion from Chevron, and Chevron produced $34.1 billion. So the lines above are, if anything, on the high side.

For investors seeking regular income and long-term capital appreciation, retail real estate investment trusts (REITs) offer an interesting opportunity. Realty Income O and Regency Centers REG share a focus on tenants providing everyday goods and services, helping shield rental income from fluctuations in discretionary spending. Both have established dividend programs, investment-grade credit ratings and opportunities to expand their rental income through new investments.
However, the similarities largely end when it comes to their growth strategies. Realty Income primarily owns freestanding properties under long-term net leases, with exposure extending beyond retail into industrial and other assets across the United States and Europe. Regency Centers concentrates on grocery-anchored shopping centers in attractive suburban U.S. markets, where leasing, tenant mix and development play larger roles.
With borrowing costs remaining an important consideration, investors need to examine how each company balances predictable income, organic growth, capital deployment and financial flexibility.
The Case for Realty Income
Realty Income's scale provides a solid foundation for rental income stability. Its portfolio spans 15,536 properties leased to 1,842 clients across 96 industries, with retail remaining the largest source of rental income. Unlike Regency, its exposure to industrial properties and international markets reduces reliance on a single retail format.
Long-term net leases generally require tenants to cover property taxes, insurance and maintenance, limiting Realty Income's exposure to rising property expenses. With an average remaining lease term of 8.5 years and occupancy of 98.8% at the end of September 2026, the company enjoys good cash flow visibility, although contractual rent increases can limit organic growth.
O's expansion beyond traditional acquisitions is particularly encouraging. Realty Income targets $10 billion of investments in 2026, while its European joint venture with KKR opens another avenue for capital deployment. Credit investments and private capital partnerships also broaden funding and investment opportunities, reducing dependence on public equity issuance.
Higher borrowing costs remain a concern, particularly given Realty Income's acquisition-driven growth model. However, available liquidity of $5.4 billion and more than 94% of pro-rata debt carrying fixed rates provide a cushion. Third-quarter investments generated a leverage-neutral spread of approximately 170 basis points, demonstrating its ability to deploy capital profitably.
For income investors, Realty Income's dividend record remains an important differentiator. In November, the company announced its 137th dividend increase since listing, lifting its monthly payout to 27.4 cents. With third-quarter dividends representing 72.6% of adjusted funds from operations (AFFO), the company retains some flexibility to fund further growth.
The Case for Regency Centers
Regency Centers' investment appeal rests on its exposure to grocery-anchored shopping centers in suburban markets with favorable demographics. More than 85% of its neighborhood and community centers are grocery-anchored. An appeals court has struck down a federal law that requires workplaces to provide accommodations for pregnant women, saying Congress violated the U.S. Constitution when it passed the law in 2022.
The New Orleans-based 5th Circuit Court of Appeals issued its 9-8 decision on Friday. Advocates of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act said the decision invalidates the law in Texas, Louisiana and Mississippi, which are covered by the 5th Circuit, and could imperil the law elsewhere.
The appeals court said the act was unconstitutional because a majority of U.S. House members weren’t physically present when it was approved as part of a spending package in December 2022. At the time, the House was operating under COVID-era rules that allowed members to vote by proxy.
“The (Quorum) Clause’s text, context, original understanding and unbroken historical application all indicate that members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes — as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago and as Congress has done ever since the founding,” the court said in its decision. “‘Proxy presence’ does not count.”
A Better Balance, an advocacy group that spearheaded the law’s passage, said in a statement Friday that the circuit court ruling would likely be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court. Inimai Chettiar, the group’s president, said the ruling was “legally unsound and short-sighted.”
“The 5th Circuit has put the health, livelihoods, and economic security of millions of American women and their families at risk,” Chettiar said in a statement.
The law, which passed with bipartisan support, strengthens the rights of women to receive workplace accommodations for needs related to pregnancy and childbirth, such as time off for medical appointments and exemptions from heavy lifting.
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton sued to block the act in 2023 on grounds that it was unconstitutional. In 2024, a federal judge agreed and blocked enforcement of the law for Texas state employees.
But in 2025, a three-judge panel on the 5th Circuit court disagreed, finding that the law was properly passed under Congress’s pandemic-era rules. That decision was appealed to the full 5th Circuit.
In their dissent, the eight judges who would have upheld the law noted that no member of Congress objected that a quorum was lacking when the $1.7 trillion government funding bill was passed.
“The State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause,” they wrote.
While the law was passed during the Biden administration, the Department of Justice under the Trump administration has continued to fight Paxton’s lawsuit, which — if successful — could open the door to legal challenges of other pandemic-era laws passed by proxy.
A message seeking comment on the appeals court decision was left Sunday with the Justice Department.
